content.title: Inference from Sample Statistics
content.overview: In the SAT Math exam, the core of statistical inference is using data obtained from a sample (a subset of a population) to estimate the characteristics of the entire population. For this estimation to be valid, the sample must be representative.
learning_objectives: Understand the relationship between sample statistics (such as sample mean) and population parameters (such as population mean).
Identify the importance of random sampling in ensuring sample representativeness.
Use sample proportions or means to calculate and predict numerical ranges for the population.

sections.title: Basic Concepts of Sample and Population
sections.content:
The population is the entire set of objects under study, while a sample is a subset of individuals selected from the population. A sample statistic (such as the sample mean $\bar{x}$) is an estimate of a population parameter (such as the population mean $\mu$). If the sample is selected through random sampling, the sample is generally representative, and its statistical results can be generalized to the entire population.

![Inference Process from Sample to Population](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/aeea8480-4c7d-42b7-ae78-98b93ff6bbb6-1786502080051-957.webp)

sections.title: Proportional Inference Method
sections.content: When the proportion of a certain characteristic in a sample is known, the number of individuals with that characteristic in the population can be predicted using a proportional relationship. The formula is: (Specific quantity in sample / Total sample size) = (Estimated quantity in population / Total population size).

sections.title: Sampling Bias and Representativeness
sections.content: If a sample is not randomly selected, or if it only covers a specific subset of the population (for example, surveying only students in a library to infer the exercise habits of all students in a school), bias occurs. In such cases, the sample results cannot be generalized to the population.

worked_examples.question: A researcher randomly selected 200 voters from a city with 5,000 registered voters for a survey. The results showed that 120 of them supported Proposal A. Based on this sample, what is the estimated total number of voters in the city who support Proposal A?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Calculate the sample proportion. Support proportion = 120 / 200 = 0.6 (or 60%). Step 2: Apply this proportion to the population. Estimated population count = Total population × Sample proportion = 5,000 × 0.6 = 3,000. Therefore, it is estimated that 3,000 voters in the city support Proposal A.

common_mistakes: Incorrectly generalizing results from a non-random sample to the entire population.
Confusing sample size with population size and misplacing them when calculating proportions.
Assuming that a sample statistic must be exactly equal to the population parameter, ignoring that it is only an estimate.
exam_tips: Look for the phrase 'randomly selected' in the problem; this is the prerequisite for making population inferences.
Pay attention to whether the question asks for an 'estimate' or an 'exact' value; statistical inference usually provides an estimate.
If the sample has obvious selection bias (such as voluntary participation), the conclusion is usually unreliable.
content.recap: The key to estimating a population from a sample lies in the randomness and representativeness of the sample. By multiplying the sample proportion by the total population size, we can obtain a reasonable estimate of the population parameter.

knowledge_claims.content: A population refers to the complete set of objects under study, while a sample is a subset selected from it.
Sample statistics can only be generalized to the population if the sample was randomly selected.
To estimate the number of individuals with a characteristic in a population, multiply the proportion of that characteristic in the sample by the total population size.
The sample mean is a point estimate of the population mean and reflects the central tendency of the population.
If survey participants are self-selected (voluntary response), the sample is typically not representative.
A sample statistic is a known specific value, while a population parameter is usually an unknown target to be estimated.
Conclusions from a random sample of a specific group (e.g., school athletes) cannot be generalized to an unrelated population (e.g., all students).
In proportional inference, the formula is: Sample Part / Sample Total = Population Part / Population Total.
When solving inference problems, first check if the sampling method involved randomness.
The result of a statistical inference is an estimate, not an absolutely precise value.

items.stem: A store manager reviewed the receipts from 80 customers who were selected at random from all the customers who made purchases last Thursday. Of those selected, 20 receipts showed that the customer had purchased fruit. If 1,500 customers made purchases last Thursday, which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.A: Exactly 75 customers must have purchased fruit last Thursday.
options.B: Exactly 375 customers must have purchased fruit last Thursday.
options.C: The best estimate for the number of customers who purchased fruit last Thursday is 75.
options.D: The best estimate for the number of customers who purchased fruit last Thursday is 375.

items.explanation: The correct answer is D: The best estimate for the number of customers who purchased fruit last Thursday is 375.. Review the Exam Essentials and worked examples above, then apply the same reasoning to this question.

items.stem: A city has 50 city council members. A reporter polled a random sample of 20 city council members and found that 6 of those polled supported a specific bill. Based on the sample, which of the following is the best estimate of the number of city council members in the city who support the bill?
items.explanation: The correct answer is C: 15. Review the Exam Essentials and worked examples above, then apply the same reasoning to this question.
